outcomeNote: The win was real but only for a usage pattern the library does not encourage.
changedBeliefs: The per-execute round-trip floor inside `db.transaction()` is measurably not fundamental for the `Future.wait([tx.execute(...) x N])` shape: buffering N calls in one microtask and flushing as a single `MultiExecuteRequest` against the still-open transaction improved the focused `tx_body_write_coalescing.dart` `tx-burst-future-wait` lane -26.0% / -31.2% across two order-flipped passes with `ab_drift_check.dart` verdict REPRODUCED. This is the reproducible measurement, not the acceptance verdict — see below.

The rejection is about the *pattern*, not the numbers. `Future.wait([tx.execute × N])` inside a transaction has no strong idiomatic case in the resqlite public API: same-SQL bulk atomic writes belong on `executeBatch` (one `BatchRequest`, whole matrix runs in C), different-SQL non-atomic bursts are covered by exp 180's standalone coalescing (`db.execute` outside a tx), and different-SQL atomic bursts are rare enough that the maintenance cost of the runtime change is not warranted.

The buffered path required four load-bearing guards to stay neutral on common patterns: `_inFlightWrites` (fast path vs slow path arbiter), `hasPendingWrites` on `drainForClose` (empty-drain microtask hop guard), `List<Object?>.of(parameters)` at buffer time (parameter aliasing snapshot for the deferred send), and restoring `TraceliteProfile.traceAsync` on the fast path (Dart-side span parity for profile builds). Each was required by a measured regression or a correctness hazard Copilot flagged during PR review. That guard footprint sets a high maintenance floor on every future writer-path change — enough to justify rejection at a niche-pattern win, though not at a common-pattern win.

`MultiExecuteRequest` cross-experiment semantics: pre-213 the handler treated each write as its own autocommit under `txDepth == 0`; the buffered path required extending the same message type to also cover `txDepth > 0` (each statement inherits the outer transaction, dirty sets accumulate through the outermost commit). The handler already had the branch, but future changes to exp 180's coalescing pump now have to remember both semantics. Documented in the retained focused harness.
nextSignals: The `full savepoint-scope command batching` openCandidate remains open in the *ambitious* form only — fusing BEGIN + body + COMMIT into one writer request. Exp 213 shows the body-only variant of that vision is measurable (-26% to -31% on the burst pattern) but the remaining BEGIN/COMMIT round-trips are ~1% of tx wall in absolute terms. Do not retry the body-only variant. The full-scope variant still requires either a design that preserves callback semantics without a public API opt-in (exp 197's constraint) or a workload showing the BEGIN/COMMIT pair dominates the residual after this direction's other candidates ship — no new angle emerged from this run.

`benchmark/experiments/tx_body_write_coalescing.dart` is the durable harness for any future transaction-body write experiment. Its four lanes (tx-sequential-await, tx-burst-future-wait, tx-single-write, tx-interleaved-select) exercise the complexity/pattern trade-off explicitly: a future runner cannot claim a transaction-body write win without holding all four lanes to their exp 213 shape (the burst lane serves as the reachable-ceiling reference; the other three as neutrality guards).

Runtime prototype preserved at `archive/exp-213`. Reopen the direction if any of: (a) a production profile or downstream user report surfaces `Future.wait([tx.execute × N])`-inside-tx as a real hot path rather than a speculative shape; (b) a new design collapses the guard set from four to one (detection primitive that distinguishes burst from sequential without per-`Transaction` state, or a writer-side change that makes inside-tx multi-execute strictly cheaper without a Dart-side buffer); (c) the full savepoint-scope variant becomes tractable.

Sequential-await inside `db.transaction()` (`await tx.execute; await tx.execute`) remains bound by the per-write round-trip floor — nothing in exp 213 changes that, and users writing this common pattern paid pre-213 costs on the prototype. Future runners should not retry per-call microtask trimming (exp 170, 171 territory) without a workload that isolates that floor from the exp 213 fast-path cost.

claims.text: The per-execute round-trip floor inside db.transaction() is mechanically removable for Future.wait bursts, but the pattern has no idiomatic case in the public API — bulk atomic writes belong on executeBatch. Rejected on pattern, not numbers.
